source.title: Gamayun's Path to Multilingual Mastery: Cost-Efficient Training of a 1.5B-Parameter LLM
source.authors: A. Podolskiy; Semen Molokov; Timofey Gerasin; Maksim Titov; Alexey D. Rukhovich; Artem Khrapov; Kirill Morozov; Evgeny Tetin; C. Korikov; Pavel Efimov; Polina Lazukova; Yuliya Skripkar; Nikita Okhotnikov; Irina Piontkovskaya; Xiaojun Meng; Xue-Yi Zou; Zhen-He Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix tables and figures are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares downstream benchmark performance across models trained on different token budgets and states that raw pre-training volume does not strictly scale with performance. It does not fit or test the held-out-loss scaling laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports multilingual-training and language-sampling effects on perplexity, but these are not parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling-law tests. Its downstream comparisons concern V6; the perplexity findings are recorded under fits_no_version. It cites Chinchilla scaling laws but does not use them as its training method.
record.test_reason: This is a model technical report. It does not fit or test held-out-loss power laws, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape effects or other-modality scaling. Its downstream comparisons are across independently built models with different data, training methods, distillation and post-training, so they cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. The remark that 'raw pre-training volume does not strictly scale with performance' is a loose aside, not a controlled result bearing on V6. Chinchilla is cited only to note that small models now exceed its guidelines, and its 6TP formula is used only to estimate FLOPs in Table 8.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a 1.5B multilingual model trained on about 2.5-2.6T tokens with two-stage pretraining (balanced multilingual, then English-enriched high-quality data) reaches state-of-the-art multilingual and Russian results among 1-2B models. They also conclude it still lags models with about 10x more compute on advanced knowledge and math. They draw no conclusions about loss-scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a multilingual model and compares benchmark results; it does not run the original scaling-law sweeps, fit loss curves, or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Training language mix and sampling strategy affect reported development loss and perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Gamayun (1.47B, 2.6T tokens) matches or beats 1-2B models trained on 9T-36T tokens on many English and multilingual benchmarks, but trails Qwen on MMLU and math. The models differ in data, distillation and post-training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across independently developed small LLMs, pretraining token count alone is a weak predictor of benchmark ranking when data mix and quality differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Language mix and data quality change language-specific dev loss. Multilingual training has higher English loss at equal English exposure. Adding Chinese mC4 beyond a threshold barely helps Chinese and hurts English.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data language composition and quality change language-specific pretraining loss at fixed exposure to one language.

fits_no_version.finding: Temperature and UniMax sampling raise high-resource perplexity (e.g. En 7.37 to 8.68) and lower some low-resource perplexity (Te 3.86 to 3.22 at t=3.33).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-sampling strategy redistributes pretraining perplexity across languages.

record.problems: The downstream comparisons are across independently developed models with different data, training methods, and other setup choices, so they do not isolate scale. The paper does not fit loss-scaling laws or report uncertainty for the comparisons. Several appendix values are flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Specific per-benchmark scores and the many language-by-language downstream comparisons in Tables 2–3 and 10–20 are not extracted: they are extensive, mostly do not constitute controlled scaling comparisons, and the aggregate cross-model findings relevant to V6 are recorded in r1–r2. Figure-only numeric values are unavailable in the supplied text.

untested.parts: No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal allocation estimate.
Deep-narrow configuration chosen but no controlled shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No other-modality or alternative-regime scaling fits.
No controlled scale sweep or downstream-vs-loss relation; only cross-model benchmark comparisons with confounded setups.
No analysis of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T5' and its V6 'challenges' label are not supported, because the cross-model comparisons confound scale with data, distillation and post-training. The authors themselves attribute Qwen's advantages to specialization. The token count is stated as 2.5T in the abstract and 2.6T in the tables. The Table 5 values are recoverable column-wise (En, Ru, Fr, De, Ar, Bg, Te), each column ordered proportional, t=1.43, t=3.33, UniMax.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or large-run loss predictions.
No fixed-compute sweep or estimate of compute-optimal parameter and token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form in other modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
The paper compares benchmark scores across existing models, not a controlled scale sweep or downstream performance against pre-training loss.
No analysis of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or systematic curve bending.

rows.subject: Gamayun
rows.operation_detail: Compared benchmark performance with models trained on different token budgets.
rows.measure: Performance across the considered English benchmarks
rows.value: Gamayun outperforms both in most tasks; the paper says raw pre-training volume does not strictly scale with performance.
rows.note: The comparison is between independently developed models, not a controlled scaling sweep.
rows.check: This is an uncontrolled cross-model comparison: data mix, data quality and post-training all differ, so it cannot show whether downstream performance tracks scale or loss. Unlink it from V6. Subject size and comparators are correct, and the abstract says Gamayun beats LLaMA3.2 on all considered benchmarks.

rows.subject: Gamayun
rows.operation_detail: Compared benchmark performance with models trained on different token budgets.
rows.measure: Performance across considered English and multilingual tasks
rows.value: Gamayun surpasses Qwen2.5-1.5B on a wide range of English and multilingual tasks, except MMLU; it is comparable to or better than Qwen3 on most tasks outside advanced STEM.
rows.note: The paper reports these as cross-model comparisons; training data, methods, and other setup details differ.
rows.check: The same confound as r1 applies: Qwen models differ in data and specialization (the authors suggest MMLU-skewed data), so this does not test V6. Unlink it from V6.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Comparisons among the reported 1–2B-scale models on the paper's benchmark suites
reader_labels.reason: Gamayun, trained on 2.6T tokens, outperforms models with larger stated token budgets on many reported tasks; the authors also state that raw pre-training volume does not strictly scale with performance (r1–r2).
